questions.q:
Text A – from a letter to parents by the headteacher, Ms Rivera
From September, every Year 10 student will complete 20 hours of community volunteering during the school year – for example at the food bank, the animal shelter or our partner primary school. Employers and universities tell us they value young people who show responsibility beyond the classroom. Last year, the 40 students who volunteered by choice reported feeling more confident and more connected to the local area. We will help every student find a placement.

Identify two reasons Ms Rivera gives for making volunteering compulsory. [2]
ms: Employers and universities value young people who show responsibility beyond the classroom (1)
Students who volunteered last year felt more confident (1)
Students felt more connected to the local area (1)
questions.model:
1. Employers and universities value students who show responsibility outside school.
2. Last year’s volunteers said they felt more confident and more connected to the local area.
questions.tip: Pick out reasons, not details of the scheme (20 hours, placements).

questions.q:
Text B – a post on a parents’ online forum by “BusyMum3”
Twenty hours sounds harmless, but Year 10 is already full of coursework, revision and – for some of us – part-time jobs that help pay the bills. Volunteering is wonderful when it is chosen. Forcing it turns kindness into another box to tick. And of course the 40 volunteers felt confident: they were the ones who wanted to do it in the first place. Why not reward students who volunteer instead of punishing those who can’t?

Explain what the writer implies with the phrase “Forcing it turns kindness into another box to tick.” [2]
ms: Making volunteering compulsory removes the genuine/voluntary motivation (kindness) behind it (1)
It becomes a meaningless requirement/chore students complete just to satisfy the rules (1)
questions.model: She implies that once volunteering is compulsory it is no longer a genuine act of kindness; students will just do it to meet a requirement, so it loses its value.
questions.tip: Implied meaning = what the writer suggests without saying it directly.

questions.q:
Text A – from a letter to parents by the headteacher, Ms Rivera
From September, every Year 10 student will complete 20 hours of community volunteering during the school year – for example at the food bank, the animal shelter or our partner primary school. Employers and universities tell us they value young people who show responsibility beyond the classroom. Last year, the 40 students who volunteered by choice reported feeling more confident and more connected to the local area. We will help every student find a placement.

Text B – a post on a parents’ online forum by “BusyMum3”
Twenty hours sounds harmless, but Year 10 is already full of coursework, revision and – for some of us – part-time jobs that help pay the bills. Volunteering is wonderful when it is chosen. Forcing it turns kindness into another box to tick. And of course the 40 volunteers felt confident: they were the ones who wanted to do it in the first place. Why not reward students who volunteer instead of punishing those who can’t?

TASK: Your year group will hold a debate on the new volunteering rule. Write a speech to your classmates giving your views on whether volunteering should be compulsory for Year 10 students. In your speech you should evaluate the ideas in both texts and give your own views, using ideas from both texts to support your argument. Write 250–350 words.

Write a five-point paragraph plan for your speech. Show clearly where you will evaluate each text and where your own view is developed. [4]
ms: Opening that hooks the audience and states a clear position (1)
At least one point evaluating an idea from Text A (e.g. the 40 volunteers were self-selected) (1)
At least one point evaluating an idea from Text B (e.g. workload is real, but 20 hours over a year is about 30 minutes a week) (1)
Own view developed, e.g. a compromise (choice of placements, flexible hours, exemptions/reward) (1)
Conclusion with a call to action / memorable ending (1)
questions.model:
1. Hook: “How many of you have 20 spare hours?” – my view: volunteering, yes; forced, no – unless it is flexible.
2. Text A’s benefits: employers value responsibility – convincing, but the 40 confident volunteers chose to go.
3. Text B’s workload worry: real for students with jobs, but 20 hours over a year is roughly 30 minutes a week.
4. My proposal: compulsory but flexible – wide choice, school-time options, exemptions for carers and working students.
5. Close: “Let’s make it something we choose to be proud of, not a box we tick.”
questions.tip: Plan by argument, not by text — mix ideas from both texts in your paragraphs.

questions.q:
TASK: Your year group will hold a debate on the new volunteering rule. Write a speech to your classmates giving your views on whether volunteering should be compulsory for Year 10 students. In your speech you should evaluate the ideas in both texts and give your own views, using ideas from both texts to support your argument. Write 250–350 words.

Write the opening of your speech (about 60 words). [4]
ms: Direct address to the audience of classmates (e.g. “Fellow Year 10s…”) (1)
Clear position/viewpoint on the issue (1)
At least one rhetorical device used effectively (question, triplet, anecdote, inclusive ‘we’) (1)
Register suited to peers — lively but not slangy; accurate (1)
questions.model: Fellow Year 10s, raise your hand if you have twenty spare hours this year. Not many of you? Exactly. Yet from September we are all expected to find them. I believe helping others matters – it really does – but kindness that is forced stops being kindness. Today I want to argue for a better plan: volunteering we choose.
questions.tip: A speech should sound spoken: address the audience, ask questions, use ‘we’.

questions.q:
Text A – from a letter to parents by the headteacher, Ms Rivera
From September, every Year 10 student will complete 20 hours of community volunteering during the school year – for example at the food bank, the animal shelter or our partner primary school. Employers and universities tell us they value young people who show responsibility beyond the classroom. Last year, the 40 students who volunteered by choice reported feeling more confident and more connected to the local area. We will help every student find a placement.

Text B – a post on a parents’ online forum by “BusyMum3”
Twenty hours sounds harmless, but Year 10 is already full of coursework, revision and – for some of us – part-time jobs that help pay the bills. Volunteering is wonderful when it is chosen. Forcing it turns kindness into another box to tick. And of course the 40 volunteers felt confident: they were the ones who wanted to do it in the first place. Why not reward students who volunteer instead of punishing those who can’t?

TASK: Your year group will hold a debate on the new volunteering rule. Write a speech to your classmates giving your views on whether volunteering should be compulsory for Year 10 students. In your speech you should evaluate the ideas in both texts and give your own views, using ideas from both texts to support your argument. Write 250–350 words.

Write ONE paragraph of your speech (about 100 words) that evaluates what the two texts say about the evidence from last year’s 40 volunteers. [6]
ms: Indicative content:
Text A presents the 40 volunteers’ confidence and connection as proof the scheme works
Text B points out they were self-selected — they chose to volunteer, so results may not apply to reluctant students (a strong criticism)
40 is a small group; ‘reported feeling’ is self-reported, not measured
But Text B does not disprove the benefit — some reluctant students may also discover they enjoy it
Clear judgement on how far the evidence supports compulsion

levels.d: Perceptive evaluation of ideas from both texts (e.g. questions the evidence, recognises implicit attitudes); ideas woven into a clear argument; speech conventions used confidently for peers; accurate.
Some evaluation, but often agrees/disagrees or summarises; clear structure; register mostly suits classmates; generally accurate.
Ideas repeated or copied with little evaluation; weak sense of audience; errors may affect clarity.

questions.model: Ms Rivera tells us that last year’s 40 volunteers felt more confident and connected. That sounds impressive – until you remember, as BusyMum3 points out, that every one of them chose to be there. Of course willing volunteers enjoyed it! That tells us nothing about how a student juggling a weekend job will feel. And forty people, describing their own feelings, is hardly scientific proof. Still, let’s be fair: BusyMum3 can’t prove that reluctant students wouldn’t benefit too. Some of us might be surprised. So the evidence shows volunteering can help – not that forcing it will.
questions.tip: Show you can see the strengths and limits of BOTH writers’ points before giving your verdict.

questions.q:
Text A – from a letter to parents by the headteacher, Ms Rivera
From September, every Year 10 student will complete 20 hours of community volunteering during the school year – for example at the food bank, the animal shelter or our partner primary school. Employers and universities tell us they value young people who show responsibility beyond the classroom. Last year, the 40 students who volunteered by choice reported feeling more confident and more connected to the local area. We will help every student find a placement.

Text B – a post on a parents’ online forum by “BusyMum3”
Twenty hours sounds harmless, but Year 10 is already full of coursework, revision and – for some of us – part-time jobs that help pay the bills. Volunteering is wonderful when it is chosen. Forcing it turns kindness into another box to tick. And of course the 40 volunteers felt confident: they were the ones who wanted to do it in the first place. Why not reward students who volunteer instead of punishing those who can’t?

TASK: Your year group will hold a debate on the new volunteering rule. Write a speech to your classmates giving your views on whether volunteering should be compulsory for Year 10 students. In your speech you should evaluate the ideas in both texts and give your own views, using ideas from both texts to support your argument. Write 250–350 words.

Write the final section of your speech (about 150 words), developing your own view and ending with a call to action. Use ideas from both texts. [8]
ms: Indicative content:
Own view clearly developed (e.g. compulsory but flexible; or optional with rewards; or fully compulsory with support)
Uses ideas from Text A (benefits for employers/universities, school support with placements) and Text B (workload, part-time jobs, reward rather than punish)
Practical proposal addressing objections, e.g. choice of placements, hours spread across the year, in-school options, exemptions for young carers/working students, certificates
Speech conventions: direct address, rhetorical questions, inclusive language, emphatic ending
Call to action addressed to classmates (vote, sign, speak to the head)

levels.d: Develops a convincing personal view built on evaluation of both texts; compelling speech style (direct address, rhetorical devices used with control); purposeful structure leading to a strong call to action; wide vocabulary, highly accurate.
Clear view supported by ideas from both texts with some evaluation; appropriate speech features and register; mostly accurate.
Simple view; ideas from texts mainly reported; some speech features; some errors.
Little use of texts; unclear view or audience; frequent errors.

questions.model:
So where does that leave us? I don’t think the answer is to scrap the idea. Ms Rivera is right that employers want young people who show responsibility, and the school has promised to help us find placements – that matters. But BusyMum3 is right too: some of us already work to help pay the bills, and twenty more hours could be the final straw.
Here is my proposal. Let’s keep volunteering at the heart of Year 10, but make it flexible. Let us choose where we help. Let us spread the hours across the whole year, including lunchtimes. Let students with jobs or caring duties count those responsibilities instead. And let’s reward volunteers with a certificate employers will actually read.
Kindness can’t be forced, but it can be encouraged. So when we vote today, don’t vote for “all” or “nothing”. Vote for a scheme we can be proud of – one we choose. Thank you.
questions.tip: End by telling the audience exactly what to do — and make the last line memorable.
